articles.title: Here's how Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation unfolded at Nvidia
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's shocking exit as CEO of Nvidia unspooled suddenly, yet signs of trouble had emerged much earlier.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia caps a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public.

But the seeds for Huang's downfall were planted much earlier. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International .

Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."

In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.

Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation:

Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to the Wall Street Journal.

7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.

Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.

Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information .

Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.

Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.

articles.title: Traders Turn to Kalshi Stock ‘Perps’ on Nvidia and SpaceX as Leverage Fears Grow
articles.summary: A new way for traders to place leveraged bets on stock prices is growing in popularity as questions around the outlook for AI following the US midterm electi...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A new way for traders to place leveraged bets on stock prices is growing in popularity as questions around the outlook for AI following the US midterm elections spur demand for hedging.

Perpetual futures tied to stock prices began trading on Kalshi on Nov. 5, the same day technology stocks were rocked by the worst selloff since 2020. The contracts, which offer exposure to the stock price without owning shares, have no expiration date, unlike traditional futures.

Kalshi has begun by offering perps, as they are known, on 50 large stocks, after previously rolling out similar contracts tied to the prices of commodities and crypto tokens. The trading volume on Kalshi's Nvidia Corp. perps jumped to over $100 million in the past 24 hours on Thursday, boosted by volatility around the ouster of chief executive Jensen Huang. Micron Technology Inc. volumes rose above $100 million on Nov. 9, while SpaceX traded as much as $88 million in a single day.

The perps have piqued the interest from both retail customers and hedge funds as an alternative to existing listed contracts. Kalshi offers up to 4.6x leverage on Nvdia positions and 3.5x leverage on Micron and SpaceX. They've also drawn the ire of traditional exchanges, who have questioned their legality and the lack of consumer protections.

Perps have been a feature of offshore crypto exchanges for years. That gives crypto intermediaries a leg up when it comes to offering the products now finally arriving onshore in the US.

More than two-thirds of the volume on the four largest offshore crypto exchanges comes from perps, according to Noel Kimmel, president of brokerage Ripple Prime. The company, formerly known as Hidden Road, has been clearing the contracts since 2020.

The Iran war proved an inflection point for the popularity of perps based on assets beyond crypto, said Kimmel, with clients keen to trade commodities during the weekend, when traditional futures markets were shut.

"You've seen an explosion in volume," said Kimmel, referring to clients trading perps on equities, crude and gold. "This is not a fad in my view, and I think you're going to see continued proliferation and increase in pickup across different types of asset managers."

articles.title: RBI's 6-hour reporting rule to help curb cyber threats, fraud in digital payments: Experts
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The RBI's recent comprehensive master guidelines mandating non-bank payment system operators to report unusual incidents, including
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The RBI's recent comprehensive master guidelines mandating non-bank payment system operators to report unusual incidents, including cyberattacks, critical system outages, and settlement delays, within six hours of detection are aimed at strengthening cybersecurity and curbing the growing menace of digital fraud, experts said.The directive requires all non-bank payment system operators (PSOs) to notify the central bank of such incidents in a prescribed format within the stipulated six-hour window, enabling quicker regulatory intervention and better monitoring of potential threats to the payments ecosystem.The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also mandates payment firms to report any cybersecurity incident to CERT-In within six hours of fraud detection.Experts said the move assumes significance amid the rapid expansion of digital transactions and the growing sophistication of cyber threats targeting payment infrastructure.The RBI's revised Master Directions on Cyber Resilience and Digital Payment Security Controls for non-bank Payment System Operators apply to the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), card networks, payment aggregators, prepaid payment instrument (PPI) issuers, and white-label ATM operators (WLAOs), among others.The central bank has introduced rigorous requirements for digital transactions, software security, system audits, and third-party service providers to prescribe new cyber safeguards for PSOs.Welcoming the RBI's revised and stricter cybersecurity guidelines, 63SATS Cybertech Joint MD and CEO Srinivas L said, "The RBI has turned scattered circulars into one clear rulebook, and that removes all excuses. The most significant is the requirement to hold the source code of critical third-party applications or keep it in escrow"."Many payment breaches today do not begin inside the company. They begin in vendor software that nobody inside fully understands. You cannot defend what you cannot see. Together with annual system audits, tight incident reporting, and mobile device binding, this moves cybersecurity from the IT room to the boardroom, where it belongs," he said.The RBI requires every PSO to submit an annual system audit report within two months of the end of its financial year. It retains the mandatory 12-hour cooling-off period after a customer changes their registered mobile number or email address.According to Apollo Infoways founder and CEO Ravi Prakash, "The mandatory six-hour cyber incident reporting window sends a clear message that cybersecurity can no longer remain a reactive compliance function. The RBI has taken a strategic step towards making India's digital payment ecosystem more intelligent".The revised cybersecurity framework issued earlier this month marks a significant milestone in shaping India's next generation of secure and resilient digital financial infrastructure, he added.The new rules are already in effect for large and medium PSOs. However, small PSOs have been given time until April 1, 2028, to comply."This regulation underscores the shift from reactive security to proactive cyber resilience. The six-hour reporting window will compel payment operators to invest in stronger monitoring, incident response, and risk management frameworks," Nerix Technoserve CEO Subhasis Majumdar said.The RBI has also prescribed stricter business continuity arrangements. The operators must maintain disaster recovery facilities in a different seismic zone from their primary data centres and conduct recovery drills at least twice a year.Srinivas pointed out, "India runs one of the world's largest digital payment systems, and every operator in that chain must be as strong as the bank at its end. Compliance is the floor, while resilience is the goal". Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as company conducts internal probe over Nvidia fallout
articles.summary: Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.
articles.body: Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year. Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers. The company told The Associated Press that it runs a “legitimate and lawful business” and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations “that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” It did not address specific allegations. “The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said in an emailed statement. Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” the statement said. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.” A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers. Singapore’s government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible “false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers.” Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed’s then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers. Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided “inaccurate” information to downplay her role at the company. An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China. As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.” Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated. The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le. By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan. Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was “actually still our boss” and remained involved in daily operations. The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion. In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan’s name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.” The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

articles.title: Wife buys property for Rs 1.4 crore and Dubai-based husband remits Rs 80 lakh directly into account of seller, but she gets tax notice for unexplained investment; why ITAT Mumbai ruled in her favour
articles.summary: You buy a property, part of which is funded by your husband who stays abroad and remits money in the account of the seller.
articles.body: You buy a property, part of which is funded by your husband who stays abroad and remits money in the account of the seller. But the Income Tax Department treats it as unexplained investment and adds it to your taxable income. What do you do?In one such case, a Mumbai woman’s taxable income was increased by Rs 80 lakh after the income-tax department questioned the amount paid towards the purchase of her residential property.The Mumbai bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) decided in her favour of a woman. Read on to know what happened:What the case is aboutAccording to the I-T department’s ‘Insight Portal’, the woman purchased an immovable property worth Rs 1.4 crore during the financial year that ended on March 31, 2016.The portal monitors high-value financial transactions to help detect instances of tax non-payment. The case was about Section 69 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, which deals with unexplained investments.The information originated from the sub-registrar’s office and was corroborated by data available in the tax deducted at source (TDS) statement relating to the transaction.The woman had not originally filed her income-tax return, proceedings under Section 148A were initiated. She subsequently filed her return.She explained that the investment was funded through proceeds from the sale of an earlier property and financial assistance from her husband who was residing and working in Dubai.During the assessment, the Assessing Officer examined the registered sale deed, Form 26AS and the bank accounts of the woman and the seller. After accounting for TDS of Rs 1.40 lakh, the payment towards the property worked out to Rs 1,38,60,000.The officer accepted payments totalling Rs 58.50 lakh. These included Rs 40 lakh paid on August 12, 2015, and Rs 18.50 lakh paid on August 26, 2015, which were reflected in the woman’s bank account and corresponded with entries in the seller’s account.The remaining Rs 80 lakh was disputed. The woman said her husband had paid the amount directly to the seller through a Dubai exchange bureau in two installments of Rs 40 lakh each. The seller’s bank statement recorded two credits totalling Rs 80 lakh.The Assessing Officer, however, held that this narration did not conclusively establish that the money had originated from the husband. He also noted the absence of remittance advice, exchange bureau records, transfer instructions and bank statements showing the debit from the husband’s account.Consequently, Rs 80 lakh was treated as unexplained investment. A further Rs 10,000 was added as unexplained balance consideration, taking the total addition to Rs 80.10 lakh.The Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) upheld the additions. She subsequently challenged the order in ITAT Mumbai and won reliefWhy ITAT ruled in favour of the womanAppearing before the ITAT, the woman argued that she had adequately explained the source of the entire Rs 1.4 crore investment and backed her claim with documentary evidence.She provided a detailed reconciliation of the property’s purchase price, accounting for every component of the payment, including the Rs 80 lakh transferred directly by her husband to the seller.To substantiate her case, she submitted the registered sale deed, the gift deed executed by her husband, his affidavit confirming the payments, bank statements and other relevant documents. These records, she maintained, established the movement of funds and demonstrated that the transaction was genuine.The tribunal examined the documents collectively rather than treating the absence of the original remittance records as decisive. It noted that the purchase, the registered sale deed, the seller’s identity and receipt of the consideration were not disputed.As the order stated: “There is no dispute regarding the purchase of the residential property by the assessee for a consideration of Rs.1,40,00,000/-.”The tribunal also observed that neither the Assessing Officer nor the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) had found the documents submitted by the woman to be false, fabricated or manipulated. The seller’s bank statement showed the disputed credits, while the husband’s affidavit confirmed that he had made the payments on her behalf. His identity documents and income-tax records were also placed before the tribunal.It noted: “These evidences are not isolated documents but interconnected and corroborative pieces of evidence which collectively establish the source and movement of funds forming part of the property transaction.”Another consideration was that the remittance records related to a transaction undertaken nearly ten years earlier. The tribunal found that the authorities had not conducted an inquiry with the seller or gathered adverse material from the bank to establish that the payments represented the woman’s own unaccounted money.The order stated: “More importantly, neither of the authorities has recorded any finding that the documents furnished by the assessee are false, fabricated, manipulated or otherwise lacking in authenticity.”The tribunal held that the explanation could not be rejected merely because one additional piece of corroborative evidence was unavailable when the other documents supported the transaction.It concluded: “Suspicion, however strong, cannot substitute evidence, particularly when the surrounding facts and documentary material overwhelmingly support the explanation furnished by the assessee.”It held that the woman had discharged the burden under Section 69 by establishing the contributor’s identity, financial capacity, source of funds and their use towards the property purchase. The tribunal accordingly directed the Assessing Officer to delete the entire Rs 80.10 lakh addition.The appeal was allowed.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: Meet the miso-making engineer behind Anthropic’s biggest hit
articles.summary: Boris Cherny created the Anthropic coding agent that’s made the company a driving force in the AI boom.
articles.body: Boris Cherny loves to code. So much, in fact, that he once said coding is the reason most people choose to become engineers in the first place. He’s also the reason why many tech workers may never have to write a line of code again. Cherny, 35, is the creator of Claude Code, the wildly popular Anthropic coding agent that’s made the company a driving AI force. The agent can write code, run commands, and access files to accomplish work on a user’s behalf. Claude Code was a hit with programmers and non-programmers alike in Silicon Valley, giving Anthropic an early foothold in the workplace. The tool also paved the way for Anthropic’s AI tools to play a larger role in industries like finance, legal work, marketing and more. Anthropic’s success has thrust the company into the middle of both the anxieties and optimism about AI’s impact on future jobs, and Cherny has embraced his place in that discussion. “I think for the job market, in particular for engineers, it will be disruptive,” Cherny said in an interview with CNN earlier this year. “I hope that over the long term, it’s amazing for humanity and what it unlocks.” Anthropic’s expected more than trillion-dollar initial public offering hinges on whether it can succeed in making Claude indispensable to office work. And it all started with Cherny’s Claude Code. “When people think about the IPO, they’re thinking, ‘Okay, how much room left does Claude Code have to grow?’” Willy Lee, principal at venture capital firm Neostellar, whose portfolio includes OpenAI and CoreWeave, told CNN. Here’s how Cherny, whose official title is head of applications, became a critical part of Anthropic and the broader discourse over AI’s impact on jobs. The rise of Claude Code Cherny joined Anthropic in 2024 after a nearly seven-year run at Meta, where he worked in various divisions, including Instagram, Facebook Groups and the code quality team, according to his LinkedIn. In 2022, during his Meta tenure, he and his wife temporarily moved to Japan for her work. Across the world from his colleagues in California, Cherny loved being able to code all day without the interruptions of meetings and project management tasks, he said on an episode of the tech industry podcast “The Peterman Pod” in 2025. He was one of the few engineers in Meta’s Instagram division who was coding so much. “For me, when I write code, I have an emotional relationship with it, and it’s something I think about when I’m really deep in a problem,” he said on the podcast. “I dream about it.” He spent a month experimenting with Anthropic’s models after joining the company, he told “Lenny’s Podcast,” a show about product development. In his early days at Anthropic, he mostly built prototypes to test the boundaries of what the Claude maker’s AI could do. But he reached a turning point a couple of months later when he created a command-line interface tool for Claude, which enabled the AI helper to interact directly with his computer’s operating system. Cherny made a simple request: figure out what music he was listening to. He was shocked when the tool wrote code to answer that question without being specifically told to do so. “The model was given this tool, and it figured out how to use it to answer this question that I had that I wasn’t even sure it could answer,” he said on “Lenny’s Podcast.” That side project laid the foundation for Claude Code, which surpassed $2.5 billion in run-rate revenue in February. Anthropic doesn’t disclose usage numbers for Claude Code, but a chart in the company’s S-1 filing ahead of its IPO shows revenue ramping up following Claude Code’s release. For Cherny, expanding Claude Code’s reach involves talking to real people about how they use the product. On X, Cherny replies to questions from Claude users on a weekly — sometimes almost daily — basis. It’s a habit he formed long before joining Anthropic. When he worked at Meta in California, he often showed the cafeteria workers new features to see if they were able to figure them out quickly, he told “The Peterman Pod.” “The thing that actually excites me is talking to people and understanding how we can make the product better,” he told CNN in March. “I’m just completely focused on that.” Claude Code’s effect on the AI market Enterprise AI spending accelerated in late 2025 following Claude Code’s release to the general public in May, said Ara Kharazian, senior economist at financial services company Ramp, which tracks business spending on AI. “That was the first commercially advanced version of AI that was directly productivity enhancing for a specific segment of jobs,” he said of Claude Code and other coding agents. Anthropic’s coding tool served as a jumping-off point for Claude Cowork, the company’s AI agent for general office work that can manage files and automate tasks. The idea for Cowork came after Cherny observed people and companies using Claude Code for non-technical duties. Cherny himself uses it for paying parking tickets and project management work for his team at Anthropic, he said on “Lenny’s Podcast.” Non-technical employees at the Mid-Ohio Food Collective frequently use Claude Code, according to Mark Mollenkopf, the organization’s director of software engineering. Its director of nutrition used Claude Code to build a game that’s like Tinder for food, aiming to help families choose healthier options based on their preferences. They had the idea for nearly a decade; Mollenkopf says he still has photos of a whiteboard with the initial concept from 2017. But the team has been too busy with higher priority tasks until it’s been able to have Claude Code handle it. “We’re not going to put it in production today yet, but it’s that unlock for us to be able to democratize great ideas that we’ve always had,” Mollenkopf said. Anthropic built Claude Cowork in 10 days using Claude Code. It shows how important Cherny’s brainchild has been for Anthropic’s own growth, not just drawing in more customers. Still, the company faces myriad challenges, including increased competition from OpenAI, reliance on a limited number of customers and pressure to live up to its sky-high valuation. The future of work Meanwhile, Anthropic has played a fundamental yet complicated role in the AI boom. The company has warned about the risks of AI, saying it’s capable of catastrophic consequences, yet it continues to charge ahead with new models. It worries that the economy isn’t ready for AI’s impact on jobs, yet it creates and iterates on tools like Claude Code and Claude Cowork for automating work. Cherny is at the center of that paradox. Some software engineers have grown increasingly wary of AI’s role in their jobs, with six in 10 tech workers saying they actively try to avoid using AI, according to a recent survey of 30,000 programmers conducted by tech site Stack Overflow. Some believe the tech isn’t as capable as it’s been made out to be, while others feel AI’s role in tech has led to more burnout over the pressure to perform and stay up to date on the newest technologies. Cherny has a lot of thoughts about what the future looks like. The job of a software engineer already involves doing a lot more than just coding; it entails working with designers and other teams, and figuring out what to build next. As AI takes over most coding tasks, engineers will be freed up to focus on these other parts of the job, he said. That’s why he said in March that he thinks software engineering jobs are going to start disappearing by the end of this year. “The (job) title will be maybe ‘builder,’” he told CNN. “Maybe we’ll still call them software engineers, but they’re going to do much more than engineers do today.” Cherny has emerged as somewhat of an icon among developers and engineers like Mollenkopf, who said he watches podcasts featuring the Claude Code creator and others in similar roles to learn more about AI. That’s how Mollenkopf learned about Claude Tag, a feature that lets users connect work data to Claude and then tag the AI helper in Slack. Mollenkopf said he would be “a total fanboy” if he could ever meet Cherny. What Cherny can’t predict is how long that shift could take. It’s almost the end of 2026, and software engineering jobs still exist – although they likely look different than they did several years ago. But if there’s one thing he learned during his time in Japan, it’s how to think long-term. He remembers learning to make miso, a traditional Japanese seasoning made by fermenting grains like soybeans and barley, to bond with his neighbors. It’s a hobby that starkly contrasted the fast-paced tech world Cherny was used to: a single batch could take months to make. “Miso is this interesting thing where it teaches you to think on these long-time skills,” he said. “…You just have to be very patient.”
